content: Pregnant women undergoing amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling (CVS) often worry about the pain associated with these procedures, in addition to the risk of miscarriage. Current methods to manage pain during these procedures can be broadly divided into non-pharmacological and pharmacological approaches. A systematic review was conducted to assess whether different analgesic methods effectively reduce pain during amniocentesis or CVS. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-randomized studies. A total of five studies involving 805 women were included, all of which focused on amniocentesis; no studies were identified for CVS. One RCT with 203 participants and one quasi-randomized study with 220 participants compared the use of infiltrative local anesthesia to no anesthesia. Both studies found no statistically significant difference in pain levels reported on the visual analogue scale (VAS). The mean differences (MD) in pain scores were -2.50 and 1.20, with 95% confidence intervals (CI) of -6.98 to 1.98 and -2.67 to 5.07, respectively. Another study involving 200 women compared light leg rubbing during amniocentesis to no intervention. This study found no significant change in anxiety levels (MD 0.2; 95% CI -0.63 to 1.03) or VAS pain scores (MD 0.3; 95% CI -0.35 to 0.95). A separate study with 62 participants evaluated the use of a subfreezing temperature needle during amniocentesis. The results showed no significant reduction in VAS pain scores (MD -0.8; 95% CI -1.8 to 0.2). Additionally, there was no significant difference between anticipated pain and actual pain experienced during the procedure (MD 0.4; 95% CI -0.82 to 1.62). Another trial with 120 participants compared the application of lidocaine-prilocaine analgesic cream to a placebo cream before amniocentesis. This study also found no significant difference in VAS pain scores (MD -0.6; 95% CI -1.44 to 0.24). In conclusion, the evidence suggests that pain experienced during amniocentesis is generally mild. There is currently insufficient evidence to support the routine use of local anesthetics, leg rubbing, or subfreezing needles for pain reduction during the procedure. Women undergoing amniocentesis can be reassured that the pain associated with the procedure is minimal.
